concepts.title: Dakṣa Curses the Insignia
concepts.excerpt: A great sacrifice at Prayāga. Every god, siddha and sage present. Śiva arrives with Bhavānī and the gaṇas, and everyone bows to him and takes their seats.

concepts.title: I Have Not Been Cursed
concepts.excerpt: Dakṣa has just denounced Śiva to his face in front of the assembled gods, announced that he deserves to be killed, and cursed Nandi with ash and bones and liquor.

concepts.title: What Is the Need for Rudra?
concepts.excerpt: The great sacrifice at Kanakhala is under way. Eighty-six thousand ritvijas.

concepts.title: She Heard It From a Passing Woman
concepts.excerpt: Satī is on Mount Gandhamādana having a nice time. The text is unusually specific about it — a canopy with a bathroom under it, friends around her, "engaged in many kinds of sports."

concepts.title: Worse Than Death to Go Uninvited
concepts.excerpt: Satī has just asked her husband to come with her to her father's sacrifice.

concepts.title: Sixty Thousand Gaṇas Went With Her
concepts.excerpt: Satī has permission to go. Her husband is not coming. And what he sends instead is an army.

concepts.title: He Doesn't Have a Lineage
concepts.excerpt: Satī has just asked, in front of the whole assembly, why her husband has no share.

concepts.title: Slice Off the Tongue
concepts.excerpt: Satī gets down off the bull at the gate and walks in on foot. Her mother and sisters greet her properly.

concepts.title: Satī Burns Herself by Yoga
concepts.excerpt: Everybody knows this story and almost everybody has the mechanism wrong.

concepts.title: Bhṛgu's Mantra Beats the Gaṇas
concepts.excerpt: Satī is ash. And the sixty thousand gaṇas who escorted her — the ones who left Kailāsa leaping like children, "full of curiosity about that great festival" — react at once.

concepts.title: Vīrabhadra and Mahākālī From One Hair
concepts.excerpt: His wife is dead. His army has been routed and has come home frightened.

concepts.title: Teeth for Smiling, Eyes for Winking
concepts.excerpt: Once Viṣṇu has withdrawn and Brahmā has gone home to Satyaloka, the ceremony is undefended, and the volume does something odd before the punishments start.

concepts.title: They Agreed to Fight
concepts.excerpt: Vīrabhadra has cleared the field. The gods are scattered, the guardians of the worlds have fled in ten directions, and the rishis have begged Viṣṇu to save the sacrifice.

concepts.title: I Did Not Cause the Breaking Up
concepts.excerpt: Chapter 84. Śiva has heard Nārada's account, torn a strand from his matted hair, and thrown it at a mountain.

concepts.title: Devotion Runs Through Viṣṇu
concepts.excerpt: Dakṣa is alive again with a goat's head. The gods have apologised. The sacrifice is about to be completed.

concepts.title: Six Disclosed Repairs
concepts.excerpt: Most translations are silent about their own surgery. You get the smooth English and no record of where the original resisted.

concepts.title: Viṣṇu Knew and Went Anyway
concepts.excerpt: Five chapters after the sacrifice is destroyed, the listener stops the story and asks the question a reader has been carrying for twenty chapters.

concepts.title: The Settlement, Itemised
concepts.excerpt: Everyone remembers that Dakṣa ends up with a goat's head. Almost nobody notices that it arrives as line one of a schedule.

concepts.title: Only Through Bhakti
concepts.excerpt: The battle is going badly. Vīrabhadra has broken the line, the gaṇas have driven the devas off the field, and only Indra and the guardians of the worlds are still standing.

concepts.title: He Resorted to the Path of Ordinary People
concepts.excerpt: The Satī Khaṇḍa ends with the sacrifice completed, Dakṣa restored and grateful, and everyone going home praising Śiva.

concepts.title: Kṣuva and the Varṇa Argument
concepts.excerpt: The Satī Khaṇḍa stops, five chapters after its catastrophe, to explain why Viṣṇu was even at Dakṣa's sacrifice.

concepts.title: Dadhīci's Three Boons
concepts.excerpt: Dadhīci has been killed by a king in an argument about rank, reassembled by Śukra, taught the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra, and sent off to do austerities.

concepts.title: The Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra
concepts.excerpt: The volume's fullest liturgical unit in the whole Satī Khaṇḍa is delivered standing over a dead body.

concepts.title: The March, Counted
concepts.excerpt: Vīrabhadra sets out, and the volume stops the story to do arithmetic.

concepts.title: The Omen Catalogue
concepts.excerpt: Vīrabhadra is marching. And before he arrives, the sky at Dakṣa's sacrifice does everything it can think of.

concepts.title: The Sudarśana Is Śiva's
concepts.excerpt: Vīrabhadra's army is on the horizon. Dakṣa has fallen at Viṣṇu's feet twice and begged him to save the sacrifice.

concepts.title: Viṣṇu in the Brahmana's Disguise
concepts.excerpt: King Kṣuva cannot beat Dadhīci. The sage has the vajra in his bones and cannot be killed, so the king goes to Viṣṇu, who agrees to help.

concepts.title: The Four Kinds of Devotee
concepts.excerpt: Dakṣa has been killed, restored with a goat's head, and forgiven. And the last substantial thing Śiva says to him is not about the sacrifice.

concepts.title: Disabled by Māyā, Then Held Liable
concepts.excerpt: Three sisters walk into a hall. It's a big room, a formal one, and the host is important.

concepts.title: The Arrow That Failed and the Archer Who Burned
concepts.excerpt: Everyone knows this story. The god of desire shoots an arrow at the meditating Śiva, Śiva opens his third eye, and the god of desire is burnt to ash.

concepts.title: The Mare-Headed Fire, Held Until the Deluge
concepts.excerpt: Śiva opens his third eye and the god of desire is ash in about a second.

concepts.title: Tāraka Abandons Heaven When Asked
concepts.excerpt: The most powerful being in the volume has taken over the universe. He holds a boon that makes him unkillable by anyone except a son Śiva hasn't fathered yet.

concepts.title: You Are Prakṛti, I Am Puruṣa
concepts.excerpt: A father has brought his daughter up a mountain to serve a holy man.

concepts.title: The Conduct Followed by Bad Yogis
concepts.excerpt: Himālaya has collected flowers and fruit and walked up the mountain with his daughter.

concepts.title: The Test That Śiva Commissioned
concepts.excerpt: Imagine applying for a job where the interview panel was hired by the person you'd be working for, briefed by him in private, and told to be as unpleasant as they can manage.

concepts.title: The Palm Line That Cannot Be False
concepts.excerpt: A father calls his small daughter in and tells her to bow at the visitor's feet.

concepts.title: Two Etymologies for Umā
concepts.excerpt: One of the great goddess-names of the tradition comes from a mother trying to stop her daughter doing something.

concepts.title: One Who Does What Should Not Be Done
concepts.excerpt: Most gods in most texts want to be seen as consistent. Their reliability is the product.

concepts.title: The Customary Practices of the World
concepts.excerpt: You're reading along and a god does something embarrassing. He weeps over a dead wife.

concepts.title: The Ascetic Heat That Does Not Care Who Is Burning
concepts.excerpt: A demon sits down to perform austerities, and the universe starts to burn.

concepts.title: Bhauma and the Substitute Mouth
concepts.excerpt: Śiva comes out of a very long meditation. He's been under for years.

concepts.title: The Slander That Śiva Wrote
concepts.excerpt: Menā has just seen her daughter's fiancé for the first time and he is worse than she feared — matted hair, ash, snakes, a bull.

concepts.title: Eight Arguments and a Pretty Face
concepts.excerpt: A woman is sitting on the floor of her house refusing to let her daughter get married.

concepts.title: The God With No Gotra
concepts.excerpt: Every Hindu wedding of this kind has a moment where the bride's father asks the groom to state who he is.

concepts.title: Criticize Yourself Instead
concepts.excerpt: Himālaya has become a genuinely great devotee. He has seen Śiva's true form, he wants to give his daughter to him gladly, and he is about to do it.

concepts.title: Brahmā at the Wedding
concepts.excerpt: The fire is lit. The bride is on the groom's lap. The hymns are being chanted.

concepts.title: The Disguised Test
concepts.excerpt: Somebody puts on a disguise, goes to a woman, and tries to talk her out of what she wants.

concepts.title: A Daughter Given to Avert a Threat
concepts.excerpt: Vasiṣṭha is trying to talk Himālaya into the marriage. He needs a precedent — a story about a father who gave his daughter to an unsuitable groom and was glad afterwards.

concepts.title: Padma's Curse and the Four Yugas
concepts.excerpt: Here is one of the biggest claims in Hindu cosmology: the world declines across four ages.

concepts.title: The Pavilion of Artificial Gods
concepts.excerpt: Himālaya hires the divine architect to build a wedding hall, and Viśvakarmā builds something odd.

concepts.title: The Goddesses at the Bedchamber
concepts.excerpt: The wedding is done. The couple has been walked to the chamber where the post-marriage teasing happens, and sixteen goddesses arrive to conduct it.

concepts.title: Kāma Comes Back and Apologises
concepts.excerpt: In the middle of the wedding celebrations, one person in the room is not celebrating.

concepts.title: The Dharma of a Virtuous Wife
concepts.excerpt: Pārvatī is leaving her father's house. The palanquin is ready. Her mother has dressed her.

concepts.title: She Does Not Get a House
concepts.excerpt: There is a small, persistent thread running under the Satī Khaṇḍa that most readings step over, and it is a question about property.

concepts.title: Kumāra, and the Son Who Left
concepts.excerpt: Not his mother. She was in the room where he was conceived and then she was not part of any of it.

concepts.title: Gaṇeśa: Made, Beheaded, and Promoted
concepts.excerpt: A woman is having a bath. Her husband walks in without knocking. Again.

concepts.title: Tripura, the Hardest Case
concepts.excerpt: Picture the enemy stronghold. Now read how the text actually describes it.

concepts.title: The Two Wives Who Were the Weak Point
concepts.excerpt: Two demons, twenty-five chapters apart. Both righteous rulers. Both unkillable.

concepts.title: Whole Narratives Annexed
concepts.excerpt: There is a stretch of about twenty chapters in this volume where the Śata Rudra Saṃhitā stops inventing and starts collecting.

concepts.title: The Sudarśana, Worked Eight Ways
concepts.excerpt: Viṣṇu's discus is the most recognisable object in Vaiṣṇava iconography.

concepts.title: The Swallowing of Śukra
concepts.excerpt: Not symbolically. The text is completely flat about it: Nandi grabs the enemy's priest off the battlefield "like a hawk grasping a quail," drags him across, and hands him over.

concepts.title: Uṣā, and the Sentence Passed in Advance
concepts.excerpt: A goddess tells a young woman what is going to happen to her.

concepts.title: Ardhanārī, and the Origin of Satī
concepts.excerpt: Somebody has been trying to build a world and it keeps failing.

concepts.title: The Vedas Testified and Were Overruled
concepts.excerpt: Two gods are arguing about which of them is supreme. They can't settle it between themselves, so they do the sensible thing: they call in the highest available authority and agree to abide by what it says.

concepts.title: The Śarabha and the Hide
concepts.excerpt: The demon is dead. That was the whole point of the incarnation, and it worked.

concepts.title: The Commission Pattern
concepts.excerpt: Śiva does not do the disreputable things in this corpus. Somebody else does them, and afterwards the text says he ordered it.

concepts.title: Liability and the Undisclosed Impairment
concepts.excerpt: Two beings in this corpus do something at a god's instigation and the outcomes could not be further apart.

concepts.title: Heterodoxy as a Manufactured Weapon
concepts.excerpt: Everything below is what this eleventh-century Śaiva text says about its religious rivals.

concepts.title: Texts Are Objects; Speech Fails
concepts.excerpt: Two gods are lost inside a pillar of fire. To resolve it, the four Vedas manifest and explain, in their own voices, at length, each taking a syllable of AUM and expounding it.

concepts.title: The Share-Grievance Migrates
concepts.excerpt: A daughter goes to her father's sacrifice uninvited, is slighted, says so, and dies of it.

concepts.title: Closure Without Refutation
concepts.excerpt: Five times in this volume a character stands up and makes a serious case — itemised, specific, and in three of the five, correct.

concepts.title: The Tīrtha Launders Anything
concepts.excerpt: A brahmin loses his temper and beats a calf with a tethering stake. The calf's mother decides to kill him.

concepts.title: Two Hells, Two Shadows, Two Tattva Counts
concepts.excerpt: Ask this volume where the hells are and it tells you twice. Once: below the seventh nether region, twenty-eight layers of five.

concepts.title: Three Sāmbas
concepts.excerpt: Kṛṣṇa wants a son. He goes to the sage Upamanyu, undertakes austerities, and Śiva grants him one, called Sāmba.

concepts.title: The Chakra, Given Twice
concepts.excerpt: Viṣṇu goes to Śiva because the demons are winning. He worships with a thousand lotuses, one goes missing, he offers an eye in its place, and Śiva gives him the Sudarśana.

concepts.title: Announced and Delivered
concepts.excerpt: This volume says "there are four kinds of mukti" and then names five. It says "among these four" and names a thing that is not one of the four.

concepts.title: The Four Doublets and the Four Disclosures
concepts.excerpt: Volume 2 tells the same story twice, four times over, without ever saying so.

concepts.title: The One Thing the Lens Found
concepts.excerpt: A reading instrument was pointed at this corpus before the reading started.

concepts.title: The Register Seam at Andhaka
concepts.excerpt: Most of what a reader can learn about how a compiled text was assembled has to be reconstructed by inference.

concepts.title: The Formula Count
concepts.excerpt: Anyone who reads a long stretch of this text develops the same impression: the phrases repeat.

concepts.title: The Strata This Purāṇa Carries
concepts.excerpt: A Purāṇa is supposed to be a certain kind of book: cosmology, genealogy, myth, the deeds of gods, framed as a sage telling sages.

concepts.title: The Four Śaiva Paths
concepts.excerpt: In the volume's longest chapter, a practitioner about to perform a rite stops and does something that looks, at first reading, like startling generosity.

concepts.title: The Doxography
concepts.excerpt: For most of a page, this text stops asserting anything and instead lists what people say.

concepts.title: Every Narrator Is Compromised
concepts.excerpt: Fifty-one chapters of this volume are narrated by Sanatkumāra. He is Brahmā's eldest son, an "Indra among yogis", and the voice through which the entire Umā Saṃhitā reaches the reader.

concepts.title: The Once-Glossed Layer
concepts.excerpt: A scripted census of this volume's technical vocabulary returns a number worth sitting with.

concepts.title: Criticising Śiva Outranks Homicide
concepts.excerpt: Ch 319 gives its catalogue of the worst things a person can do, and it gives it twice.

concepts.title: Objections That Block Are Engineered Around; the One That Prices Is Paid
concepts.excerpt: A sage crossing a river propositions the ferryman's daughter. She objects four times.

concepts.title: The Inventory of What You Are Giving Away
concepts.excerpt: Purāṇic cosmography is usually read as its own thing — the nether regions, the continents, the mountains, the worlds, delivered because a Purāṇa is supposed to contain them.

concepts.title: The Machine and the Amnesty
concepts.excerpt: Nineteen chapters of this volume cancel somebody's karma outright, and in eighteen of them it simply happens.

concepts.title: The Vrata He Did Not Know He Was Doing
concepts.excerpt: A hunter sits up a bilva tree all night waiting to shoot deer at the waterhole.

concepts.title: The Hells That Fit the Crime
concepts.excerpt: Four consecutive chapters of this volume describe what happens after death, and they are the most detailed penal writing in the corpus.

concepts.title: The Birth Canal Erases the Evidence
concepts.excerpt: By the seventh month the child is complete, and something happens that the volume states plainly and never revisits:

concepts.title: Nothing in the Body Is Clean
concepts.excerpt: Two chapters of this volume are a disgust-meditation on the body, which is an entirely conventional thing for a text of this kind to contain.

concepts.title: The Eight Forms and the Argument Against Harm
concepts.excerpt: Most of this volume's ethics arrives as a list: do this, do not do that, and here is the hell attached.

concepts.title: Who May Be Initiated
concepts.excerpt: Ask this volume who is allowed in and you get three incompatible answers, none of which acknowledges the others.

concepts.title: Dīkṣā Is a Varṇa Promotion
concepts.excerpt: Most of what this literature says about varṇa mobility is denominated in lifetimes.

concepts.title: The Praṇava Diagram
concepts.excerpt: A liṅgam is a smooth vertical stone on a pedestal. There is not much to it, structurally: a base, a middle, an upper part, a top.

concepts.title: The Mendicant's Burial
concepts.excerpt: The Kailāsa and the Vāyavīya do not agree about how many tattvas there are, or how many components the syllable AUM has, or what the Virajā oblation purifies.

concepts.title: Two Boats, Two Rocks
concepts.excerpt: The volume's best image for why a teacher has to be qualified is four words long and it is not about competence:

concepts.title: The Siddhi Cascade
concepts.excerpt: Late in the volume there is a passage that does something the rest of the corpus keeps failing to do.

concepts.title: The Yogi's Limbs and Impediments
concepts.excerpt: Two chapters near the end of this volume stop being a Purāṇa and start being a manual.

concepts.title: The Guru's Cow
concepts.excerpt: Something unusual happens in six chapters of this volume, and it happens without anybody appearing to arrange it.

concepts.title: The Corpus of the Disqualified
concepts.excerpt: A tradition tells you two things about who it is for. It states rules, and it tells stories.

concepts.title: Sudyumna, Twice
concepts.excerpt: One named figure. One volume. Two accounts of how he came to change sex, and they agree about nothing except that it happened.

concepts.title: The Lineage That Swallowed the Śākyas
concepts.excerpt: Deep in a chapter of future kings — the kind of passage a reader's eye slides over, name begetting name for two pages — this sentence goes past:

concepts.title: Dhundhu, Who Breathes Once a Year
concepts.excerpt: A sage cannot live in his own hermitage, and the reason is not a rival, a curse or a war.

concepts.title: One Story, Two Gods
concepts.excerpt: The gods have won a war and they are pleased with themselves. A figure appears that none of them recognises.

concepts.title: What the Demon Knew
concepts.excerpt: The most accurate piece of theological reasoning in this volume is spoken by the villain, in the middle of a battle he is losing, about the goddess who is about to kill him.

concepts.title: The Goddess Assembled
concepts.excerpt: The gods have lost. A buffalo demon holds heaven and has taken over the offices of the sun, the moon, the wind, death and fire, and performs all of them himself.

concepts.title: Two Kauśikīs
concepts.excerpt: A goddess is produced from another goddess's body, and the volume explains her name twice.

concepts.title: The Courtship That Was an Inventory
concepts.excerpt: Two servants see a woman on a mountain and go back to report to their king.

concepts.title: Kill Us Where the Earth Is Not Flooded
concepts.excerpt: Two demons have fought a god for five thousand years and then wrestled him.

concepts.title: Only What a Character Asks
concepts.excerpt: A sage has been listening to a long lecture.

concepts.title: Named Circularity, Unnoticed Contradiction
concepts.excerpt: A goddess is being asked personal questions by a god she would rather not answer.

concepts.title: The Apparatus Is the Translator's
concepts.excerpt: Open the volume at the page about donations. A sentence tells you that a certain merit follows from listening to "any one of the thirty-six Puranas."

concepts.title: The Saṃhitā That Grew
concepts.excerpt: Most old books do not tell you how long they are meant to be. This one does.

concepts.title: The Kailāsa Is a Different Book
concepts.excerpt: For three hundred and sixty-five chapters this book has been telling you things that happened.

concepts.title: Two Numbering Systems That Are Not Unique
concepts.excerpt: You write down a reference. Chapter 388. It is the chapter where the text publishes the size of every one of its own sections — a table, twelve rows, summing to exactly a hundred thousand.

concepts.title: The Devotees Who Exist Only in the Endnotes
concepts.excerpt: Somewhere in the middle of the second volume there is a roll-call of the saved.

concepts.title: The Pāśupata Charter
concepts.excerpt: Somewhere behind this volume there was a real religious order — ash-smeared, staff-carrying, liṅga-worshipping, organised around a discipline with a stated duration and a named founder.

concepts.title: The Five Faces and the Eight Forms
concepts.excerpt: Chapters 230 and 231 are the volume's most systematic passage.

concepts.title: The Twelve Jyotirliṅgas
concepts.excerpt: > "Somanatha in Sourashtra; Mallikarjuna in Shrishaila; Mahakala in Ujjayini; Amareshvara in Omkara; Kedara on the slopes of the Himalayas; Bhimashankara in Dakini; Vishvesha in Varanasi; Tryambaka on the banks of Goutami; Vaidyanatha in a cremation ground, Nagesha in the forest of Daruka; Ramesha in Setubandha; and Ghushmesha in Shivalaya."

concepts.title: The Liṅga Gazetteer
concepts.excerpt: Chapter 273 is one paragraph. Inside it are roughly seventy name-tokens for Śiva liṅgas — sixty-six of them distinct — each with a place attached or a fruit promised, and almost none with a story.

concepts.title: The Practice Layer
concepts.excerpt: Somewhere inside these 134 chapters is a functioning practitioner's manual: eight or nine named mantras, seven named vratas with durations and calendar dates, half a dozen named weapons, and at least one named single-purpose technique.

concepts.title: Mleccha, Five Ways
concepts.excerpt: Everything below is what an eleventh-century Śaiva text says about categories of people it places outside its own order — mleccha, antyaja, bhilla, caṇḍāla.

concepts.title: The Indemnity Clause Runs Hot
concepts.excerpt: There is a phrase this volume reaches for whenever it is about to describe a god doing something a god should not be able to do.

concepts.title: The Self Archetype: The Integrative Center and Its Relationship to Ego in Trauma
concepts.excerpt: Jung's most fundamental archetypal discovery was the Self — not the ego (the conscious, individual "I"), but a deeper organizing principle that transcends the individual while including it.

concepts.title: Shame as Survival System
concepts.excerpt: Shame is not a moral failing or a character defect. It is an evolved survival mechanism: the nervous system's response to the threat of tribal exclusion.

concepts.title: Stoic Dichotomy of Control
concepts.excerpt: What is eph' hēmin: your judgments, intentions, desires, responses — the activity of the governing rational faculty (hegemonikon).
